study.title: Lancet LBP Series 1: burden, course, and why the source is rarely found
study.evidence_note: Narrative synthesis of reviews and cohorts. Frames the whole lumbar playbook; tests no treatment. Core messages match later guidelines.
study.confidence_note: Full text read from your PDF; second pass made 10 corrections. Messy Table 1–2 cells not quoted. Cited reviews not re-checked.
study.impact_line: Most settle by 6 weeks, but most still have some pain at 12 months. Scans don't find the source.
summary: Narrative review by the international Lancet LBP Series working group (paper 1 of 2)
Draws on systematic reviews, large cohorts, guidelines and GBD 2015; no formal appraisal of sources
Persistence better explained by pain intensity, leg pain, distress, fear and social factors than tissue findings
Treatment is covered in paper 2 of the series, not here
study.bottom_line: Treat back pain as variable and recurrent, not unrelated episodes. Don't promise a tissue diagnosis. Screen early for pain intensity, distress and leg or multisite pain.

design: Narrative review, Lancet Series paper 1 of 2
No protocol, PRISMA flow or risk-of-bias assessment
setting: Mostly high-income evidence, some low- and middle-income data
methods.primary_outcome: None; descriptive (burden, causes, course, risk factors)

results.detail: Under 28% of cases are severe but carry 77% of disability. About 540 million people at any time. Body text uses YLD; key messages and Figure 3 label the same figure DALYs. Card follows the GBD source (YLD).

results.result: ~37%, peaks mid-life, higher in women; ~40% of 9–18 year olds
results.meaning: Common at all ages, incl. adolescent athletes

results.result: Most improve a lot by 6 wk; mean pain 6/100
results.detail: From a review of 33 cohorts (11,166 people).

results.meaning: Aim for function and control, not zero pain
results.detail: Cited to two prognosis reviews jointly. The ~35% pain-free at 12 months is derived (100 − 65), not stated in the paper.

results.result: ~33% recur; authors say estimates aren't robust
results.detail: 7 studies, 1,780 people. No CI given in the text.

results.result: Bulge, extrusion, Modic 1, spondylolysis more common with pain
results.effect: e.g. bulge OR 7.5 (1.3 to 44.6); extrusion 4.4 (2.0 to 9.7)
results.meaning: Common without pain; can't name the source
results.detail: Degeneration OR 2.2 (1.2 to 4.2; 34% without vs 57% with pain), protrusion 2.7 (1.5 to 4.6), Modic 1 4.0 (1.1 to 14.6), spondylolysis 5.1 (1.7 to 15.5). CIs crossing 1: fissure 1.8, HIZ 2.1, any Modic 1.6, spondylolisthesis 1.6, canal stenosis 20.6 (0.1 to 798.8). Heterogeneity mostly high.

results.meaning: Single red flags have very low specificity
results.detail: Australian primary-care sample. 2 of 11 were inflammatory disorders. About 80% of people with acute back pain have at least one red flag.

results.result: Positive LRs mostly 1 to 2.5; fear-avoidance evidence conflicts
results.meaning: Inform the plan, don't predict a person
results.detail: Table 2 is not systematic. Fear avoidance median LR 2.2 at 3–6 mo and 2.5 at 12 mo (4-study review), but a 21-study review found no link with pain or activity (it did with work outcomes). Pain intensity LR 1.7 then 1.3; leg pain 1.4; catastrophising OR 1.56 (1.05 to 2.33); previous episodes LR 1.0 to 1.1.

results.meaning: Over half unexplained; real performance likely lower
results.detail: Validated models (appendix) consistently include pain intensity, distress, and leg or multisite pain. The 43% comes from a 50-study review (33,089 people) of seven development samples.

key_numbers.label: Still in some pain at 12 months
Acute LBP with at least one red flag

pico.p: People of any age with low back pain, mostly from high-income countries
pico.i: Not applicable (descriptive review of burden, causes, course and risk factors)
pico.o: Prevalence, disability, natural history, imaging associations, prognostic factors

limits: Narrative review: source studies not systematically selected or appraised
Prognostic table is explicitly not from a systematic review
Published 2018, so later trials and guidelines aren't included

full_text.why: Read in full from Curt's PDF.

how_to_apply: First session: most improve a lot by 6 weeks; most still have some pain at 12 months; a third relapse.
Frame success as function, confidence and flare control, not pain-free.
Asked the cause: say the exact source usually can't be found; scan findings are common without pain.
Treat Atlas 'discogenic' as a working label, not a confirmed source.
Don't image routinely; image when red flags or a surgical question point to it.
Screen early: pain intensity, distress, leg or multisite pain. Use a positive screen to shift the plan, not label.
applies_to: Adults and adolescents with non-specific LBP, with or without leg pain
Lumbar playbook: educate and classify steps
not_for: Diagnosing a tissue source, e.g. discogenic pain
Ruling serious pathology in or out from one flag
Fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina or suspected axSpA: specific pathways

High heterogeneity for 7 of 11 MRI findings; fear-avoidance reviews conflict.
Same population and outcomes; some low- and middle-income data may not transfer.

clinical_significance: No treatment effect, so no MCID or NNT applies
Useful facts: natural history, and weak diagnostic value of scans and single red flags
Prognostic LRs mostly 1 to 2.5: small shifts in probability
comparator_fairness: MRI case-control comparisons are pain-free people; age under 50 matters
alternative_explanations: MRI and risk-factor links may reflect confounding, reverse causation or age
12-month recovery includes natural history and regression to the mean
Authors say causal roles of risk factors remain unclear
spin: Little: abstract and conclusions match the body
'Health care adds to burden in high-income countries' is opinion, not a finding
Call for cost-effective, context-specific strategies isn't backed by data here
fit_with_evidence: Consistent with the Atlas lumbar playbook
Cites Brinjikji 2015 (MRI) and Foster 2018 (treatment); guidelines advise against routine imaging
Doesn't support a confirmed discogenic diagnosis: no accepted reference standard
external_validity: ✓ Natural history, imaging stance, psychosocial screening
would_change_my_mind: A validated test that identifies a disc source in active adults
New cohorts showing recovery well away from ~35% pain-free at 12 months
A trial showing early imaging improves outcomes

Quantified statements on red flags, imaging, natural history

Wide CIs and high heterogeneity for MRI estimates

verification.external_searched: PEDro title search 2026-11-04: none (doesn't index narrative reviews). No Cochrane or AMSTAR rating found.

study.patient_explanation: Most back pain settles over a few weeks, but it often hangs around at a low level or comes back, and that's common. Scan findings show up in lots of people with no pain, so we focus on getting you moving and confident.
open_questions: Which short tool best screens fear and distress in active adults?
Do natural-history figures differ in athletes and highly active adults?
Could a validated rule ever justify a discogenic label?
Does a structured programme after recovery cut relapse?
key_findings: Leading cause of disability worldwide: 60.1M YLD in 2015, up 54% since 1990
Specific pain source can't be identified in nearly all cases
Most improve by 6 wk; 65% still have some pain at 12 mo; ~33% recur within a year
MRI findings are common without pain; imaging hasn't been shown to improve outcomes
Serious pathology 0.9% in Australian primary care; single red flags discriminate poorly

sources.citation: Hartvigsen J, Hancock MJ, Kongsted A, Louw Q, Ferreira ML, Genevay S, et al. What low back pain is and why we need to pay attention. Lancet 2018;391:2356-67.
